title: FAST-GC: A Fully Adaptive Self-Tuning Ground Classification Algorithm for Multi-Platform LiDAR Sensors
content: Ground-point classification (GPC) is a fundamental step in LiDAR data processing because classification errors propagate into digital terrain models (DTMs), height normalization, vegetation structure metrics, and other derived products. Existing GPC algorithms depend on user-defined parameters whose effectiveness can vary with terrain complexity, vegetation structure, sampling density, and sensor-platform acquisition geometry. We present FAST-GC, a fully automated and self-tuning GPC algorithm that does not require scene-specific parameter calibration. FAST-GC was evaluated through complementary experiments encompassing a controlled six-site comparison with established ground-filtering algorithms, terrain-complexity and slope stress testing, systematic point-density reduction across 20 ALS sites, cross-platform ALS–ULS–TLS assessment, and large-area processing. Across the controlled comparative sites, FAST-GC maintained high ground completeness while limiting commission error, with its advantage over the established algorithms becoming increasingly pronounced as terrain complexity increased. At slopes of 70–80°, FAST-GC achieved a DTM mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.00 m compared with 3.12–12.75 m for the evaluated algorithms. Extended assessment across 20 ALS sites further demonstrated stable performance under systematic sampling-density reduction: reducing median density from 9.84 to 3.84 pts./m²  maintained F1 ≈ 0.97, intersection over union (IoU) ≈ 0.95, and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) ≈ 0.85, while DTM MAE increased only from 0.07 to 0.11 m. Independently reconstructed 0.5 m terrain surfaces from ALS, ULS, and TLS observations showed strong cross-platform correspondence despite substantial differences in acquisition geometry and sampling conditions (R² and concordance correlation coefficient ≥ 0.99; RMSE = 0.10–0.16 m). Large-area processing of 382 ALS tiles (~23 km²) further demonstrated stable tile-wise execution and automated terrain-product generation. Collectively, the results show that GPC performance is governed not only by point-wise classification agreement but also by the ability to preserve terrain morphology under increasing topographic complexity, reduced sampling support, and contrasting acquisition geometries. By adapting terrain-support estimation internally rather than requiring scene-specific parameter calibration, FAST-GC provides a reproducible and scalable framework for heterogeneous and multi-platform LiDAR processing.
